prompt: A home-goods marketplace is deciding what evidence to show beside each product claim. Name the kind of attribute each claim describes.

cases.text: A bath towel measures 70 by 140 centimeters.
cases.explanation: Dimensions can be checked from the specification table before buying.

cases.text: A memory-foam pillow stays comfortable through a whole night of side sleeping.
cases.explanation: Comfort is only known after sleeping on it, which is where buyers' reviews help.

cases.text: The cotton in a set of bed sheets was grown without synthetic pesticides.
cases.explanation: A buyer cannot verify how the cotton was farmed even after using the sheets, so a third-party certification is needed.
Weight is an objective specification available before purchase.

cases.text: A scented candle fills a living room with a pleasant smell without smoking.
cases.explanation: Scent and burn quality are learned only by lighting the candle.

cases.text: A rug's maker offset all the carbon emitted while shipping it.
cases.explanation: No amount of use reveals the offset, so it rests on audits and certification.

prompt: A shopper compares four blenders on a marketplace. Match each review dimension with the observation that reflects it.

pairs.match: One blender has 3,100 reviews while another has only nine.
pairs.explanation: Volume is the count of posted reviews, a cue of popularity and statistical reliability.

pairs.match: One blender averages 4.4 stars and another averages 3.2 stars.
pairs.explanation: Valence is the average star rating or overall sentiment.

pairs.match: Half of one blender's ratings are 5 stars and most of the rest are 1 star.
pairs.explanation: Variance is how spread out ratings are, and a split between the extremes signals a polarizing product.

pairs.match: A blender's reviews from the previous month mention a new motor that overheats.
pairs.explanation: Recency tracks how fresh the latest reviews are and can reveal a recent change in the product.

question_text: An outdoor-clothing retailer will add a 10 dollar credit to its review request email and wants as many buyers as possible to write a review. Which message should it pair with the credit?
hint: Think about whom the review is said to help and how that fits with a payment from the retailer.
correct_answer_citation: When a solicitation message frames review writing around helping other shoppers, it activates intrinsic pro-social norms, whereas pairing mismatched financial framing with altruistic appeals can dull the marginal lift of both levers.

options.option_text: "Your review helps us improve our business, and we will thank you with a 10 dollar credit."
options.option_explanation: Paying the buyer to help the company that pays turns the request into a low-paid transaction, which dulls the credit's lift.

options.option_text: "Your review helps other shoppers like you choose the right jacket, and we will thank you with a 10 dollar credit."
options.option_explanation: Correct. Framing the review around helping fellow shoppers keeps the pro-social motive while the credit adds an extrinsic one.

options.option_text: "Write a review and receive a 10 dollar credit," with no reason given.
options.option_explanation: A credit alone works, but it leaves out the altruistic appeal that can add to its effect.

options.option_text: It does not matter, because a financial incentive overrides whatever the message says.
options.option_explanation: The effect of the incentive depends on how the message frames it, so the two levers interact.

prompt: A skincare brand is drafting review offers. Sort each offer into the kind of incentive it is.

cards.text: A 5 dollar credit for every honest review, whatever its rating.
cards.explanation: The reward is paid simply for completing a review.

cards.text: One entry into a monthly gift-card draw for each submitted review.
cards.explanation: The entry does not depend on the review's rating, length or votes.

cards.text: An extra 3 dollars when the review includes a photo of the product in use.
cards.explanation: The payout rises with a media attachment, a performance metric.

cards.text: A 15 dollar bonus once the review collects 25 helpful votes.
cards.explanation: The payout depends on helpfulness votes cast by readers.

cards.text: A full refund for buyers who post a 5-star rating.
cards.explanation: Rewarding only a 5-star rating biases valence and breaks consumer protection rules.

cards.text: A free sample for customers who raise a 3-star rating to 4 stars or more.
cards.explanation: The reward depends on the review becoming more positive.

prompt: A marketplace's trust team reviews flagged cases. Name the manipulation in each one.

cases.text: A listing that once sold ballpoint pens, with 6,000 ratings, now sells a cordless drill and still shows all 6,000 ratings.
cases.explanation: Swapping the variation keeps the old rating count for an unrelated new product.

cases.text: Shoppers in a chat group are refunded through a payment app after posting 5-star reviews of a phone case.
cases.explanation: The seller is buying fabricated positive reviews and paying for them off the platform.

cases.text: Residents receive unordered packets of seeds, and each address soon appears beside a verified 5-star review.
cases.explanation: Cheap parcels to real addresses create verified purchase records for fake reviews.

cases.text: Within one night, 300 new accounts give a rival's yoga mat 1 star, and the mat drops off the first results page.
cases.explanation: A coordinated flood of 1-star ratings is used to sink a competitor's rank.

cases.text: A desk lamp's page is changed to list a coffee grinder, keeping the lamp's 4.7-star average.
cases.explanation: The new item inherits the rating earned by a different product.

question_text: A shopper asks an AI agent to buy a well-rated electric toothbrush. Brush A shows 5.0 stars from 6 reviews, and Brush B shows 4.5 stars from 2,800 reviews with a rating breakdown and verified purchases. What risk does bounded algorithmic rationality create here?
hint: Consider what the agent may pay attention to if it is not told to examine the evidence behind each average.
correct_answer_citation: However, under bounded algorithmic rationality, agents can over-weight salient summary statistics or vivid extreme reviews unless prompted to evaluate rating distributions and verified sample sizes systematically (Wadi & Ma, 2026a).

options.option_text: The agent will refuse to choose because the two averages differ.
options.option_explanation: Differing averages do not stop an agent from choosing. The risk is how it weighs them.

options.option_text: The agent will always pick Brush B, because agents read every review.
options.option_explanation: Agents read sample passages and summary statistics, not every review.

options.option_text: The agent may favor Brush A's salient 5.0 average unless it is prompted to weigh the six-review sample against the large, verified distribution of Brush B.
options.option_explanation: Correct. Without prompting to check distributions and sample sizes, the salient summary statistic can dominate.

options.option_text: The agent will ignore the AggregateRating schema and rely only on product photographs.
options.option_explanation: Agents evaluate the structured AggregateRating schema along with review passages.
